Lessons.Title: Choose a Scale
ExplanationParagraphs: Original 2021 Illustrative Mathematics K–5 Grade 3 Unit 1 Lesson 6, CCSS 3.MD.B.3, teaches how to choose an appropriate scale for a categorical BAR GRAPH. Lesson timeline: 10-minute warm-up, 20-minute pattern blocks Activity 1, 15-minute seasons Activity 2, 10-minute synthesis, 5-minute Cool-down. First-party diagrams and teaching text are Edulytics-authored; mathematical source semantics and exact category values are retained.

Warm-up — Notice and Wonder: Bar Graph Scales. The THREE original Lifespan of Pets vertical graphs present Cat 16, Dog 13, Guinea Pig 6, Goldfish 10, Python 30 YEARS under different scales: vertical axis 0–30 by 1, 0–60 by 2 and 0–300 by 10. Students compare how those axes affect apparent bar height and interpretability without changing any original quantity. Partner quiet think, discussion and teacher-recorded observations are open, not machine-graded.

Activity 1 — Represent Pattern Blocks. The original 2021 first-edition SVG (asset ID 7053kvgtyqg9pibtx7gto33ajaea) was retrieved and its visible geometric SVG paths counted. It contains 26 DISTINCT visible green triangles, 5 orange squares, 15 red trapezoids and 10 yellow hexagons, totaling 56 blocks. It declares 27 green fill paths, but one is an EXACT DUPLICATE at the same location; do not count the invisible overdraw twice. Edulytics displays 56 independently constructed shapes in a different layout and palette. The original students choose from Mai's scale 2, Noah's scale 5 or Priya's scale 10, graph four category counts and justify their selected interval; teacher assesses graph construction, counting strategy and partner critique.

Activity 2 — Represent More Data in a Scaled Bar Graph. The 2021 school table lists favorite time of year: Winter 24, Spring 13, Summer 40, Fall 22. Learners pick a scale (such as 2, 5 or 10), ENTER the height of each of the four bars and generate a scaled BAR graph from their own values only after submitting. The teacher inspects a zero-aligned vertical plot, accurate bar endpoints BETWEEN numbered ticks (never round 13, 24 or 22), title and category labels. Work independently for about 5–7 minutes, then share in groups for about 2–3 minutes, using MLR8 partner reasoning; the graphs feed into the next lesson.

Lesson synthesis (10 minutes) happens BEFORE Cool-down. Invite students to compare scale choices and explain what helps them decide on an appropriate graph interval. The ORIGINAL 2021 five-minute Cool-down 'Reflection on Bar Graphs and Scale' contains TWO SEPARATE OPEN writing questions: why they chose the scale for their last graph, and what they learned that will help with their next scaled graph. Teacher reviews both distinct responses; they must NOT be replaced by a graded fictional-club number drill. AFTER Cool-down, conduct the Math Community reflection on the most important classroom norm and why. Optional teacher-directed centers are Sort and Display Stage 3 Scaled Graphs and Five in a Row Stage 6 Addition/Subtraction; independent Edulytics club numerics remain clearly marked optional extra practice.

KeyConcepts.Title: Data values stay constant as the axis changes
KeyConcepts.Definition: Three scaled vertical graphs can display the exact same categorical values.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Compare the number axis, label and real value, not just visible relative bar height.
KeyConcepts.Example: Cat remains 16 on a graph up to 30, 60 or 300; Python stays 30.

KeyConcepts.Title: Pattern-block source inventory
KeyConcepts.Definition: The first-edition picture shows four shape families with mathematically observable frequencies.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Count distinct visible instances; identical overprinted source SVG path records do not represent additional objects.

KeyConcepts.Title: Scale selection: 2, 5 or 10
KeyConcepts.Definition: A chosen step controls numbered tick intervals on the graph.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Choose a step reaching the largest value while preserving precise placement even between ticks.
KeyConcepts.Example: For 26 triangles, a five-unit axis to 30 fits, with the bar endpoint at 26, just above the 25 tick.

KeyConcepts.Title: Season graphs from the original table
KeyConcepts.Definition: A scale changes presentation but not the school survey counts.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Bar heights equal Winter 24, Spring 13, Summer 40, Fall 22 exactly. The pupil creates the graph.
KeyConcepts.Example: On a 0–40 graph numbered in fives, Spring =13 is between 10 and 15.

KeyConcepts.Title: Teacher-reviewed reflection
KeyConcepts.Definition: Source Cool-down assesses reasons, not a uniquely correct computation.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Preserve both original open questions and the later Math Community reflection as teacher-reviewed.
KeyConcepts.Example: A child might prefer fives to reduce axis labels, but must explain how the other values can still be read.

WorkedExamples.Title: Warm-up — fixed counts on three differently scaled axes
WorkedExamples.Question: Do these three pet graphs represent different lifespans?
WorkedExamples.Method: Read data values and vertical maximum separately.
Steps: List cat 16, dog 13, guinea pig 6, goldfish 10, python 30.
Notice the three vertical maxima 30, 60 and 300.
Compare one-unit, two-unit and ten-unit tick gaps.
Explain why the plotted bars become relatively shorter as the vertical axis maximum increases.
WorkedExamples.Answer: No, all three show the identical five category values.
WorkedExamples.Check: 16+13+6+10+30=75 is the sum of those displayed category values, not a claim about a pet survey.

WorkedExamples.Title: Activity 1 — source-verified pattern counts and scale
WorkedExamples.Question: Use the pictured 26 triangles, 5 squares, 15 trapezoids and 10 hexagons to create a scaled graph.
WorkedExamples.Method: Count from the displayed independently authored shape collection, then choose 2, 5 or 10 and plot exact bar endpoints.
Steps: Add the tallies to check 56 visible blocks.
Choose a scale, for example five from 0 to 30.
Place 26 between ticks 25 and 30; place 5, 15, 10 on their exact ticks.
Explain to a partner the readability trade-off between steps two, five and ten.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Example valid scale: five; source graph heights 26, 5, 15 and 10, accurately plotted.
WorkedExamples.Check: 26+5+15+10=56. The pupil's justification and drawn graph need teacher assessment.

WorkedExamples.Title: Activity 2 — seasonal bars
WorkedExamples.Question: Choose an axis scale and plot the source school survey Winter 24, Spring 13, Summer 40, Fall 22.
WorkedExamples.Method: Make a vertical graph, with zero baseline and meaningful interval labels.
Steps: Choose ticks of five to 40, as an example rather than the only permissible answer.
Place Winter 24 between 20 and 25, Spring 13 between 10 and 15.
Draw Summer exactly at 40 and Fall 22 between 20 and 25.
Label category names, graph title and numeric vertical axis.
WorkedExamples.Answer: The exact season bars are 24, 13, 40 and 22.
WorkedExamples.Check: 24+13+40+22=99. Verify exact values independently and teacher-review the bar positions.

WorkedExamples.Title: Original Cool-down — source's two open reflections
WorkedExamples.Question: Why did you choose your scale, and what idea will you use next time?
WorkedExamples.Method: Respond to each of the two prompts as an evidence-based explanation.
Steps: Refer to the greatest value in the season table.
State your chosen interval and why it helps readability.
Explain how you avoided rounding between ticks.
Write a separate takeaway about future scale choices for teacher review.
WorkedExamples.Answer: There is no single numeric correct response; the teacher evaluates each explanation independently.
WorkedExamples.Check: Both distinct source reflections remain open/teacher-reviewed, not machine-passed.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Treating a longer vertical axis maximum as a larger animal count.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: A scale changes the fraction of plotting space, never the category data.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Match pet values across all three original axis intervals.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Counting the source's duplicated triangle path as an additional physical block.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The exact same green triangle path is drawn twice on top of itself and has one visible location.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Count 26 visible triangles, not 27 SVG path entries.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Rounding 26 to 25 or 30, and Spring 13 to 10 or 15, to sit on a numbered tick.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Scaled bar charts must preserve exact data even between ticks.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Place bar endpoints in the correct intermediate position.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Counting optional club calculations as the original source Cool-down.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The original lesson uses TWO distinct written reflection questions, not club-number questions.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Present both source reflection prompts before Math Community; grade them by teacher rubric.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Assuming correct typed bar heights prove teacher observed a learner's strategy.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Scale explanations, visual labels, collaborative questioning and Math Community require human evidence.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Keep separate teacher review instead of treating machine-checked numerics as proof.

SummaryPoints: 2021 timeline: warm-up 10, pattern blocks 20, favorite seasons 15, synthesis 10, original reflection Cool-down 5 minutes.
Three pet graphs represent 16,13,6,10,30 years under vertical scales 0–30/1, 0–60/2, 0–300/10.
2021 visible pattern SVG: 26 triangle, 5 square, 15 trapezoid, 10 hexagon, total 56; first-party equivalent redraw, no copying.
2021 season table: Winter 24, Spring 13, Summer 40, Fall 22; learner creates exact bar endpoints and chooses 2, 5 or 10.
10-minute synthesis BEFORE source two-question open Cool-down; AFTER Cool-down reflect on Math Community norms.
Teacher-only centers Sort and Display Stage 3 and Five in a Row Stage 6 are mapped but not fabricated as digital student completions. Publisher original artwork not reused.
